newsitem.title: UK: Oil prices ease as UN nears Iraq aid plan approval.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices ease as UN nears Iraq aid plan approval.

text.p: Oil markets trod water on Monday as last week's rally inspired by strong gasoline demand in the United States was seasoned with caution prompted by signs of progress towards a resumption of Iraqi exports next month.

London benchmark Brent crude futures shed five cents to $18.48 a barrel by 1643 GMT as New York gasoline dealers took profits but volumes were thin as the market waited for the United Nations to approve a revised food distribution plan submitted by Baghdad.

An extension of Friday's bullish gasoline sentiment pushed prices higher in early dealing before news Iraq had submitted annexes to the plan to the United Nations on Monday, clearing the way for approval in the next few days, sent the market lower.
"The news from Iraq is the reason we're seeing a lid on the market," said a broker.
Under the terms of the deal, Iraq is allowed to sell up to $2 billion of oil over 180 days in two equal 90-day instalments.

After exporting about 700,000 barrels per day (bpd) in the first six months, Iraq was given permission for a second round starting on June 8 but Baghdad has delayed the restart of oil exports, insisting on revisions to the way aid is distributed.
The delay has coincided with strong demand for crude from U.S. refiners running flat out to meet healthy gasoline consumption and prevented prices from extending this year's $7 a barrel slide.

Iraq's ambassador to the U.N. Nizar Hamdoon said on Monday his country was still hoping the United Nations would change its mind and allow Baghdad to make up time lost since June 8 by putting back the start.
"The Security Council agreed on Thursday that the date for oil sales starting is when the Council approved Resolution 1111 (the second round)... June 8," a senior U.N. official said.
U.N. officials said on Monday they expect to approve the food distribution plan this week.

But the delay in restarting the second round means Iraq will either have to sell oil at a rate of between 1.5 million and two million bpd during August and the first week of September or forego some of its quarterly allotment, Western diplomats said.
Hamdoon would not be drawn on whether Baghdad would accept the Security Council position and try to sell its $1 billion allotment by September 5, forfeit some sales or adopt another course of action.
"I cannot comment on that yet. First we will wait for approval of the aid plan and then we will see what is the position of Baghdad," he said.
Despite the apparent progress on the resumption of Iraqi exports, traders said prices may hold steady for a little while longer given tightness of supply on U.S. gasoline markets.
"There are no real signs that the (gasoline) rally will end yet, at least while the August (NYMEX) contract is alive," said brokers GNI.
Also proving mildly supportive was news of a technical problem at the North Sea Forties pipeline, Britain's biggest export stream.

The system, which was running at an average 840,000 bpd over the previous 24 hours, was shut for an hour on Monday morning but some of the fields feeding the stream were closed for significantly longer.
